records.name: Durango
records.current_summary: Durango sits on both sides of Mexico's protective-law gradient. It passed Decreto 356, formally typifying transfeminicide in state law, part of the wave of state statutes (following Nayarit's March 2024 first-in-country definition) that recognise gender-motivated killing as an aggravated offence. Yet Human Rights Watch's March 2025 country review lists Durango among the six states that have reformed nothing to create a legal gender-recognition procedure - a mismatch between symbolic criminal law and the administrative vacuum that leaves identity documents permanently unfixable and is the most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico. As with the other state transfeminicide statutes, national reporting finds the laws advancing 'in law but not in sentences', so they mark official climate rather than enforcement.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024): documents how the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police stops, denial of documents and institutional mistreatment - the country's clearest case of administrative erasure, cited to establish what a state without any procedure does to trans residents and visitors.

The Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024): Mexico City criminalised transfeminicide with sentences up to 70 years after the 2016 killing of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro whose attacker was released despite footage and witnesses and remains at large; activists call the law a watershed in one of Latin America's deadliest countries for trans people, while the reporting notes convictions lag the statute - the benchmark for judging other states' transfeminicide laws.

records.name: Guanajuato
records.current_summary: Guanajuato is one of the country's sharpest contrasts: among the most lethal states and one of the most advanced legislatures. It recorded the second-highest state count in the 2021 national report of violent deaths of LGBT+ people (9, in a year led by another state with 10), and has remained among the top states in subsequent years. It was simultaneously the first state in the country to pass a comprehensive sexual-and-gender-diversity law - approved unanimously by all 32 deputies across the governing and opposition parties on 15 February 2024 and published 7 June 2024 - and it amended its penal code the same year to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. But Human Rights Watch devoted a March 2024 documentary to discrimination against trans people in Guanajuato over identity documents, and a federal court had to order the state congress in June 2024 to create a rights-respecting recognition procedure - the statute book moved faster than the administration that must apply it.

records.name: Guerrero
records.current_summary: Guerrero passed one of the country's fullest sub-national rights statutes: Ley No. 239 on the Recognition and Rights of the LGBTTTIQ+ Community (2025), a comprehensive recognition-and-rights law alongside its 2024 penal-code alignment with transfeminicide provisions. The Supreme Court struck down the statute's adults-only limitation in 2026, extending its reach to minors - confirming both the state's protective-law ambition and the judiciary's role in completing it. No dedicated incident or enforcement reporting was found for the state beyond these statutes, which is itself notable in one of the country's most violent regions; the protective framework is legislative rather than documented in practice.

records.name: Jalisco
records.current_summary: Jalisco combines high recorded lethality with legislative resistance. In the 2024 national state-by-state count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people it sits immediately behind the top two jurisdictions (the federal capital first with 17, including 11 trans women). Its congress then voted down extending gender recognition to minors in March 2025 in open defiance of a Supreme Court ruling obliging states to provide recognition procedures - placing Jalisco among the states actively refusing to implement the national standard for trans people's documents. Border-area reporting from the neighbouring state also documents rising attacks in municipalities on the Jalisco frontier, with gay-men killings attributed to named municipalities there.

records.name: Mexico
records.current_summary: Among the most lethal states on record and institutionally behind its own law: the 2021 national hate-crime count recorded 7 violent deaths of LGBT+ people in the state, whose penal code has recognised anti-trans bias crimes since 2021 (Article 211 Bis reform). Its 2021 civil-code reform created an administrative gender-recognition procedure but excluded under-18s; after the Supreme Court struck that exclusion down in June 2023 the congress had still not complied as of March 2025 - among the clearest legislative non-compliance cases in the country.

records.name: Nayarit
records.current_summary: A legislative pioneer whose statutes outrun their enforcement: Nayarit created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure in 2017 and in March 2024 became the first state in Mexico to typify transfeminicide, with sentences up to 60 years - a step Mexico City followed with the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024. Press reviews find such statutes have produced few convictions, so they measure official posture more than protection; beyond these laws there is no dedicated incident or enforcement reporting for the state.
